explanations.explanation: Night it is, baker. Nehemiah says, "I set out at night with a few men." (Nehemiah 2:12) No crowds, no parade, no questions. I think a quiet look around is easier when nobody's watching, like sneaking one warm cookie off the cooling rack.

Sunrise would have been a fine time for a walk, but that's not what the text says. Nehemiah, the man the king sent to Jerusalem, says, "I set out at night with a few men." (Nehemiah 2:12) He's out under the dark sky, not the morning sun. I'd have needed a flashlight and a very good excuse.

Midday means the sun is high and everybody can see you. That's not this trip. Nehemiah, the man the king sent to Jerusalem, says, "I set out at night with a few men." (Nehemiah 2:12) Nobody strolls out at noon on a secret mission, friend.

Right, baker. Nehemiah says, "I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem." (Nehemiah 2:12) The plan stays in his heart for now. Keeping a secret that big for three days? I can't keep a secret about what's in the oven for three minutes.

The priests are a good guess, but they're not in on it yet. Nehemiah says, "I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem." (Nehemiah 2:12) Later the text says he hadn't yet told the Jews or priests or nobles or officials or any other workers (Nehemiah 2:16). So the priests were still waiting right along with everyone else.

Not even the nobles, friend. Nehemiah says, "I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem." (Nehemiah 2:12) Verse 16 lists the nobles right there among the people he hadn't yet told (Nehemiah 2:16). Nobody got a sneak peek at this batch.

Gates, baker. Nehemiah inspects "the walls of Jerusalem that had been broken down and the gates that had been destroyed by fire." (Nehemiah 2:13) Broken walls and burned gates, and he sees it all with his own eyes. That's a lot to take in by night, and I think it's a heavy sight.

Towers are in this chapter later, but not in this verse. Nehemiah inspects "the walls of Jerusalem that had been broken down and the gates that had been destroyed by fire." (Nehemiah 2:13) So the word is gates. Burned ones, and he looks them over.

I get why you'd say houses, but the text doesn't. Nehemiah inspects "the walls of Jerusalem that had been broken down and the gates that had been destroyed by fire." (Nehemiah 2:13) It's the gates that burned. This verse says nothing about houses, so I won't add any.

Animal, baker. The text says "there was no room for the animal under me to get through." (Nehemiah 2:14) The only animal with Nehemiah is the one he's riding (Nehemiah 2:12). So the ride stops where the space does. Tight squeezes happen to me too, mostly when I try to fit one more cookie on the tray.

The men did fine, friend. The trouble was "no room for the animal under me to get through." (Nehemiah 2:14) It's the animal Nehemiah is riding that can't fit. The text doesn't say the men had any trouble at all.

There's no cart in this story. The text says "there was no room for the animal under me to get through." (Nehemiah 2:14) And the only animal with Nehemiah is the one he's riding (Nehemiah 2:12). One rider, one animal, one very narrow spot.

That's it, baker. Nehemiah says, "Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace." (Nehemiah 2:17) Notice the words "Come, let us." He doesn't say "you go do it." He puts himself right in the work with them.

Nobody's packing up. Nehemiah says, "Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace." (Nehemiah 2:17) He wants to fix the city they have. Nothing in his speech is about moving.

explanations.answer: Ask the king to send builders
explanations.explanation: A good thought, but Nehemiah has a different plan. He says, "Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace." (Nehemiah 2:17) The "us" is the people standing right there. They're the builders.

True, baker. Nehemiah says, "Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace." (Nehemiah 2:17) The wall is the job, and no more disgrace is the goal he names. Nehemiah says "we," so he counts himself in.

It's actually true. Nehemiah says, "Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace." (Nehemiah 2:17) So rebuilding the wall is how they'd stop being a disgrace. He says "we" and counts himself in.

Not quite, friend. The people don't ask for time. They say, "Let us start rebuilding," and "they set their hands to this good work." (Nehemiah 2:18) No committee, no "let me sleep on it." I wish my cookie ideas got that kind of yes.
False is right, baker. The people reply, "Let us start rebuilding," and "they set their hands to this good work." (Nehemiah 2:18) They say yes and get started. No stalling, and I love it.

Yep. The text says "they mocked us and ridiculed us." (Nehemiah 2:19) Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem hear about the work and start laughing at it. It's the kind of laughing that isn't any fun for the people on the receiving end.

explanations.answer: Offer to help with the wall
explanations.explanation: No offers of help here, friend. The text says "they mocked us and ridiculed us." (Nehemiah 2:19) Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem show up with questions and scorn, not hammers. And Nehemiah tells them they have no claim in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:20).
No attack yet in this passage. The text says "they mocked us and ridiculed us." (Nehemiah 2:19) Words are all that fly in these verses. They ask, "Are you rebelling against the king?"

Rebelling, baker. They ask, "What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?" (Nehemiah 2:19) That's quite a question to throw at people holding bricks. They're asking it as part of their mocking.

Complaining isn't the word. They ask, "What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?" (Nehemiah 2:19) Rebelling is a much bigger charge than complaining. Nobody was grumbling in this scene, they were building.

Sinning is a different charge entirely. They ask, "What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?" (Nehemiah 2:19) They're talking about the king, not about right and wrong. The word you want is rebelling.

Right, baker. Nehemiah answers, "The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success." (Nehemiah 2:20) He doesn't point to himself or to his plan. He points to God, and then he gets back to building.

The king helped, and Nehemiah told the people what he had said (Nehemiah 2:18). But Nehemiah's answer is different: "The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success." (Nehemiah 2:20) So success comes from God, not from the king.

The people of Judah will do the work, but they aren't the ones Nehemiah names. He says, "The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success. We, His servants, will start rebuilding…" (Nehemiah 2:20) The builders build, and God grants the success.
Not at all, friend. Nehemiah tells them, "…you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem." (Nehemiah 2:20) He says the opposite of what the card says. That's a pretty direct answer to mockers.

False is right, baker. Nehemiah says, "…you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem." (Nehemiah 2:20) He doesn't give them an inch. He answers Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem plainly and goes back to the work.
